by selective laser melting


To cite this article: P Ponnusamy et al 2018 IOP Conf. Ser.: Mater. Sci. Eng. 377 012167



View the article online for updates and enhancements.





                            This content was downloaded from IP address 179.198.47.184 on 28/11/2026 at 08:51International Conference on Mechanical, Materials and Renewable Energy                  IOP Publishing
IOP Conf. Series: Materials Science and Engineering1234567890‘’“”377 (2018) 012167  doi:10.1088/1757-899X/377/1/012167





High strain rate behaviour at high temperature of AlSi12
parts produced by selective laser melting


          P Ponnusamy1,2, S H Masood1,2, D Ruan1,2, S Palanisamy1,2, R A Rahman
              Rashid1,2 and M A Kariem3

                 1Faculty of Science, Engineering and Technology, Swinburne University of Technology,
               Melbourne, Australia 3122
                2Defence Materials Technology Centre, Melbourne, Australia 3122
                      3 Faculty of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Bandung Institute of Technology,
              Ganesha Street no. 10, Bandung, West Java 40132, Indonesia

                Abstract. High  strain  rate dynamic behaviour  of metals  is normally studied  at room
                temperature using a split Hokinson pressure bar (SHPB) equipment. This paper presents an
                  investigation on a high strain behaviour at a high temperature for AlSi12 aluminium alloy parts
               produced by selective laser melting (SLM) additive manufacturing technology. Dynamic tests
                 of parts were carried out at room temperature as well as at 200 C using the split Hopkinson
                 pressure bar  to understand the dynamic behaviour of AlSi12 and the results were compared
                with quasi-static compression tests carried out at the same temperatures. The effect of flow
                   stress due  to an  increase  in  temperature was  analysed.  Further  observations  through
                 microstructure were  also conducted. Negative  strain  rate  effect was observed  at room
                 temperature, while positive strain rate effect was observed at high temperature.

1. Introduction
Selective laser melting (SLM) has become a widely used additive manufacturing (AM) process for 3D
printing of metal parts in a range of materials including steels, titanium and aluminium alloys.  In the
SLM process, parts are produced directly from CAD file data using laser melting and rapid cooling of
metal powder spread on a platform in a layer-by-layer fashion. One of the advantages of SLM includes
geometric freedom and  realisation  of  intricate  parts,  normally  not  possible by  conventional
manufacturing processes. SLM involves rapid cooling of the melt pool, resulting in a very fine
microstructure and with enhanced mechanical properties  [1]. The SLM  is one of the few AM
processes, which has been successful in processing certain aluminium alloys. However, processing of
aluminium alloys by AM offers several challenges due to its poor powder flowability, high thermal
conductivity and atmospheric oxidation  [2]. Louvis  et  al. [3] have reported the  difficulties in
processing of aluminium alloy by high power SLM and considered the changes that can be made to
the SLM process so as to reduce the laser power required and increase the laser scanning rates, while
still producing components with a high relative density. They reported that combination of laser power
and scan speed causes the balling effect in the aluminium parts, and oxidation was the other major
problem, which must be eliminated for parts with 100% density. More in-depth understanding of the
mechanical behaviour of aluminium parts made by SLM is essential for its potential application under
various loading conditions in several industry sectors such as aerospace and automotive.

Several investigators have attempted to characterise the mechanical behaviour of aluminium alloys
processed by selective laser melting. Chou et al. [4] carried out a study to manufacture AlSi12 alloy


              Content from this work may be used under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 licence. Any further distribution
               of this work must maintain attribution to the author(s) and the title of the work, journal citation and DOI.
Published under licence by IOP Publishing Ltd                    1International Conference on Mechanical, Materials and Renewable Energy                  IOP Publishing
IOP Conf. Series: Materials Science and Engineering1234567890‘’“”377 (2018) 012167  doi:10.1088/1757-899X/377/1/012167



parts using a pulsed selective laser melting (SLM) process as opposed to continuous SLM process and
showed that pulse SLM allowed for greater control over the heat input offering more optimization
possibilities of the microstructure and hardness in the parts. Vora et al. [5] investigated the processing
of AlSi12 parts using an anchor-less processing on SLM by pre-heating of the powder bed, which
resulted in reducing the residual stress in aluminium parts. Wang et al. [6] analysed the fabrication of
AlSi12 components using SLM process under various atmospheric conditions in the SLM chamber.
They studied the effect of Ar, N2 and He gases and found that the density and hardness of parts made
were not affected by changing the atmosphere. However, Ar and N2 were found to produce better
ductility than He in the aluminium parts. Siddique et al. [7] investigated the effect of SLM process
parameters and post-heat treatment on the microstructure and the resulting fatigue behaviour of AlSi12
parts. They reported that base plate heating affects the microstructure and mechanical behaviour of
parts produced by SLM and mechanical properties are found to be better than those by conventional
methods. In another study, Siddique et al. [8] conducted a very high cycle fatigue and fatigue crack
growth behaviour of AlSi12 produced by SLM. They reported that the fatigue behaviour improved
through base-plate heating and fatigue mechanism was controlled by micro-porosity. Prashanth et al.
[9] studied the effect of heat treatment on tensile properties of AlSi12 alloys by SLM and reported that
yield strength of SLM samples reduced from 260 MPa to 95 MPa and the fracture strain increased
from 3% to 15% due to isothermal annealing. The microstructure after annealing became coarser. Li et
al. [10] investigated the effect of solution heat treatment time on tensile strength of AlSi12 parts by
SLM and found that the increase in tensile properties of AliSi12 parts in SLM could be attributed to
the refined eutectic microstructure. They also observed an increase in ductility by 25% approximately.

Published literature reveals that no research seems to have been made to study the dynamic behaviour
of aluminium parts processed by SLM process. In this paper, the focus is on the high strain rate
behaviour as there are many practical applications such as high speed machining, mining machines,
and situations such as automotive impacts, where strain rates can be as high as in the range of 102 /s to
104 /s subjected to various temperatures. Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar (SHPB) has been used in this
study to characterise the dynamic compressive behaviour  at high temperature of AlSi12  parts
produced by ProX200 selective laser melting machine.

2. Material and Methods
2.1 Selective Laser Melting
The selective laser melting (SLM) machine used was ProX200, which was supplied by 3D Systems
equipped with a fibre laser. The working principle of SLM has been described in [3]. The aluminium
alloy AlSi12 powder was supplied by 3D systems, which was used to produce fully dense samples on
the ProX200 for quasi-static compression tests and high strain rate compression tests.  The process
parameters used for preparing the samples in the SLM are: Laser power: 285 W, which is the 95 % of
laser power, scanning speed of 1000 mm/s, and defocus distance of -4 mm. Along with other
parameter, the layer thickness was 40 µm. Argon gas of high purity was used inside the SLM chamber
in order to purge oxygen and to avoid possible contamination.

Cylindrical specimens of dimensions Ø10 mm × 10 mm were built horizontally in the SLM build plate
and they were machined to Ø 8 mm × 8 mm size with an aspect ratio of 1.0 for quasi-static as well as
dynamic tests. Necessary support anchors were built in order to maintain the mechanical stability of
built samples. Also, the scan strategy followed was hexagonal pattern. The samples were polished
using Auto-polisher, Struers Tegramin-25 and in order to reveal the microstructure, the etchant used
was the sodium hydroxide and water, which had the composition of 10 gm of NaOH pellets and 90 ml
of H2O. Also, optical microscope of model Olympus 

## 2. ponnusamy2018highstrainrate pages 3-7 (Context ID: pqac-00000008)

gh purity was used inside the SLM chamber
in order to purge oxygen and to avoid possible contamination.

Cylindrical specimens of dimensions Ø10 mm × 10 mm were built horizontally in the SLM build plate
and they were machined to Ø 8 mm × 8 mm size with an aspect ratio of 1.0 for quasi-static as well as
dynamic tests. Necessary support anchors were built in order to maintain the mechanical stability of
built samples. Also, the scan strategy followed was hexagonal pattern. The samples were polished
using Auto-polisher, Struers Tegramin-25 and in order to reveal the microstructure, the etchant used
was the sodium hydroxide and water, which had the composition of 10 gm of NaOH pellets and 90 ml
of H2O. Also, optical microscope of model Olympus BX61 was used to analyse the microstructure.

2.2 Quasi-static tests
A 50 kN MTS machine was used for quasi-static testing at the room temperature, and a 100 kN
INSTRON machine with a heated chamber was used for a quasi-static testing at a high temperature.
The rate of deformation was 1 mm/ min and the corresponding strain rate was 2 × 10-3 s-1 for tests at




                                                         2International Conference on Mechanical, Materials and Renewable Energy                  IOP Publishing
IOP Conf. Series: Materials Science and Engineering1234567890‘’“”377 (2018) 012167  doi:10.1088/1757-899X/377/1/012167



room temperature as well as at high temperature. ASTM E9 standard was followed for arriving at the
sample standard with aspect ratio 1. A temperature of 200 C was maintained in the chamber for quasi-
static studies at high temperature.

2.3 Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar
Figure 1 shows the schematic view of the spilt Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) apparatus used for
high strain rate testing [11]. In general, the SHPB apparatus consists of five key elements namely two
symmetrical pressure bars, a bearing and alignment fixture to allow free movement of the bars, a
compressed gas launcher, generally a pair of strain gauges mounted on both input and output bars, a
data acquisition system to mainly record the strain wave data. The test sample is sandwiched between
incident bar and transmission bar. To minimize the effect of friction between the specimen and the
bars, a thin layer of molybdenum disulfide lubricant is applied between the contacting surfaces. When
the striker bar impacts the incident bar,  it creates an elastic compressive pulse, referred to as an
incident pulse. This incident pulse will propagate through the bar towards the sample. When the pulse
reaches the sample, a portion of the pulse is reflected back into the incident bar due to the impedance
mismatch between the incident bar and the specimen. The remaining portion of the pulse will be
transmitted through the sample and into the transmission bar.





                         Figure 1. Schematics of SHPB [11].

Axial resistive strain gages are attached on the surface of the incident and transmission bars at the
midpoint of the bars. These strain gages provide time-dependent strain pulses of the bars. In one of the
oscilloscopes, the velocity is recorded. Both the incident and the transmission bars are made of
maraging steel, whose nominal yield strength and elastic modulus are equal to 2310 MPa and 190 GPa
respectively. Their diameter and length are 14.5 mm and 1200 mm, respectively. The striker bar,
incident bar and transmission bars are of identical diameter and made of same steel. However, the
striker bar length of 300 mm has been used. The sample temperature was increased to 200 °C by
heating only the specimen, while keeping the  incident, transmission and  striker bars  at room
temperature. Essentially, the bars were brought in to contact with the specimen just a fraction of
second before an impact of the striker bar. The sample mounted between incident bar and transmission
bar is assumed to have a dynamic stress equilibrium and the sample undergoes constant strain rate
while deformed [12]. The signals from the strain gauges are amplified and recorded by high speed
digital oscilloscope. The relative magnitudes of these incident, reflected and transmitted strains are
combined to generate the dynamic stress strain curve for the specimen [13]. Figure 2 shows the
voltage magnitudes of incident, reflected and transmission pulse obtained from the incident and
transmitter bars for an AlSi12 specimen. From this data set the strain rate vs. strain is calculated.





                                                         3International Conference on Mechanical, Materials and Renewable Energy                  IOP Publishing
IOP Conf. Series: Materials Science and Engineering1234567890‘’“”377 (2018) 012167  doi:10.1088/1757-899X/377/1/012167





       Figure 2. Volt-time diagram of incident, reflected and transmitted signals of SHPB test.

3. Results and discussion
Figure 3 shows stress-strain curves for the quasi-static and dynamic (SHPB) compression tests at room
temperature for AlSi12 parts made by SLM. Two test samples were tested for each case. The strain
rate for quasi-static stress was 2 × 10-3 /s and the maximum strain rate for dynamic curves was 750/s.
A negative strain rate effect is observed in Figure 3, where the flow stresses are larger for the quasi-
static stresses when compared to dynamic curves. This effect was due to micro-cracks observed in the
microstructure as shown in Figure 4 as well as due to the thermal softening caused by adiabatic
heating.





  Figure 3. True stress vs. true strain curves at room temperature for quasi-static and dynamic tests.

In Figure 3, the quasi-static as well as dynamic flow stresses are found to be consistent, as the same
applied forces in terms of quasi-static tests and the velocity for SHPB tests were maintained.





                                                         4International Conference on Mechanical, Materials and Renewable Energy                  IOP Publishing
IOP Conf. Series: Materials Science and Engineering1234567890‘’“”377 (2018) 012167  doi:10.1088/1757-899X/377/1/012167





Figure 4. Microstructure of AlSi12 tested samples at room temperature for (a) dynamic studies; and
(b) quasi-static studies.

In Figure 4(a), dynamic studies shows that lesser number of pores and no cracks were observed.
However, in Figure 4 (b), more oval shaped pores and cracks propagating along the grain boundaries
were observed. Also, coarse grains were found along the grain boundaries compared to grains found
inside the laser tracks in both the dynamic and quasi-static studies.





           Figure 5 True stress vs true strain at 200 C for quasi-static and dynamic tests.

Figure 5 shows stress-strain curves for the quasi-static and dynamic (SHPB) compression tests at 200o
C temperature for AlSi12 parts made by SLM. The positive strain effect was observed in Figure 5
where the maximum strain rate attained for the dynamic flow stress was 1500/s and the quasi-static
stress was 2 × 10-3 /s. The dynamic flow stress at 200 C was found to increase significantly when
compared to the quasi-static flow stress.





                                                         5International Conference on Mechanical, Materials and Renewable Energy                  IOP Publishing
IOP Conf. Series: Materials Science and Engineering1234567890‘’“”377 (2018) 012167  doi:10.1088/1757-899X/377/1/012167





  Figure 6. Microstructure of AlSi12 at 200o C for (a) dynamic studies; and (b) quasi-static studies.

In Figure 5, it is noted that a positive strain rate occurred due to the rate controlling mechanism, which
was also mentioned as a thermally activated diffusion [14]. The strain rate sensitivity with respect to
an increase in strain rate was found to be higher, which could be due to the nature of AlSi12 produced
by SLM. Also, both the temperature and strain rate affect the strength and deformation characteristics
that was  influenced by  dynamic  recrystallization  [15].  Figure  6  shows  the  microstructure
corresponding to the positive strain rate effect, which reveals that no pores are found and grain
boundary was well defined. The microstructure revealed that the grain boundaries became narrow in a
horizontal orientation after quasi-static testing. The pores observed in all the cases were observed to
have closed after dynamic testing, as the applied force was compressive by nature.

4. Conclusions
The quasi-static stress strain as well as dynamic stress strain curves at high strain rate compressive
loads conducted at room temperature and at a high temperature for SLM built AlSi12 parts were found
to be repeatable and consistent. The effect of strain rate on the flow stress at room temperature and
high temperature at 200° C was analysed. From the quasi-static and dynamic stress strain curves,
negative strain rate effect was observed for specimens tested at room temperature and positive strain
rate effect was observed for specimens tested at high temperature.

Scalmalloy®

P. Jakkula1     · G. Ganzenmüller1,2     · F. Gutmann1,2 · A. Pfaff2 · J. Mermagen2 · S. Hiermaier1,2


Received: 25 June 2020 / Accepted: 22 March 2021 / Published online: 7 April 2021

Abstract
This work investigates the influence of strain rate on the stress/strain behaviour of Scalmalloy. This material is an aluminium–
scandium–magnesium alloy, specifically developed for additive manufacturing. The bulk yield stress of the material processed
by Selective Laser Melting is approximately 340 MPa which can be increased by heat-treating to approximately 530 MPa.
These numbers, combined with the low mass density of 2.7 g/cm3, make Scalmalloy an interesting candidate for lightweight
crash-absorbing structures. As this application is inherently dynamic, it is of interest to study the loading rate sensitivity,
which is difficult to predict: Al–Sc alloys exhibit classic strain rate sensitivity with an increased yield stress at elevated strain
rates. However, Al–Mg alloys are known to show the contrary effect, they exhibit less strength as strain rate is increased. To
answer the question how these effects combine, we study the dynamic behaviour at four different strain rates ranging from
­10−3 to 1000 /s using servo-hydraulic and split-Hopkinson testing methods. The resulting data is analysed in terms of strain
rate sensitivity of tensile strength and failure strain. A constitutive model based on a simplified Johnson–Cook approach is
employed to simulate the tensile tests and provides good agreement with the experimental observations.

                This work is licensed under CC Public Domain Mark 1.0Abstract


This thesis investigates the strain-rate-dependent mechanical response of Al6061 alloys additively

manufactured by laser-beam powder bed fusion (PBF-LB). The research aims to understand how

process-induced porosity, post-processing heat treatments, and microalloying affect the quasi-

static and dynamic response of Al6061 alloys. The research combines systematic mechanical

testing with multi-scale characterization. Experimental investigations are supported by digital

image correlation (DIC) for full-field strain mapping, X-ray microscopy (XRM) for porosity

measurement, electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction (XRD) for microstructural and phase

analysis.


PBF-LB Al6061 samples were built with process parameters from the literature to achieve good

part density and mechanical performance. The as-built samples and those subjected to direct aging

(DA), annealing (AN), T6 heat treatment (solution treatment (ST) + artificial aging), and hot-

isostatic pressing (HIP) were characterized. XRM and SEM analyses revealed residual lack-of-

fusion porosity between 3% and 5%, indicating that the investigated post-processing strategies did

not densify PBF-LB Al6061. EBSD analysis showed minimal variation in grain size or texture

among heat-treatment conditions, indicating that these strategies did not modify the grain structure.

Quasi-static and dynamic compression tests carried out on a material testing system (MTS) and a

split-Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) revealed that the as-built and DA samples had the highest

flow stresses and hardness, while the AN, T6 and HIP samples showed significant softening. All

conditions exhibited a positive strain-rate sensitivity and a consistent reduction of the Poisson’s

ratio during dynamic loading, suggesting an inertial confinement and pore-collapse mechanism.

These results showed that traditional heat treatments are of limited benefit and that residual

porosity significantly controls the mechanical strength.

                                                                     iiBuilding on this baseline, additional investigations were performed to determine whether alloy

modifications could mitigate the limitations related to porosity and enhance the mechanical

performance of PBF-LB Al6061. Two variants of PBF-LB Al6061 were investigated: a scandium-

doped Al6061 powder produced by ball milling (Al6061-Sc), and a ceramic-reinforced Al6061

powder known as Al6061-RAM2 containing 2 vol% of inoculant particles of Ti/B4C. The Al6061-

0.3%Sc samples were fabricated with process parameters investigated through a DOE based

parametric study. Al6061-RAM2 samples were fabricated with the manufacturer recommended

parameters. Quasi-static and dynamic tensile tests were performed using an Instron universal

testing machine and a tensile split-Hopkinson pressure bar (T-SHPB) over strain rates ranging from

10-4 to 2.8 × 103 s-1. Strain evolution was recorded using a high-speed camera and analyzed by

DIC. The two modified alloys exhibited considerably different microstructural and mechanical

responses. The Al6061-RAM2 material exhibited lower porosity (0.28 ± 0.18%), finer equiaxed

grains, higher hardness as well as substantially higher tensile strength and ductility than the

Al6061-Sc material. On the contrary, the Al6061-Sc samples showed a high porosity level (4.92 ±

0.82%) with a large interconnected pore cluster, leading to premature fracture and severely limited

tensile performance. The results showed the strength of both materials was higher under dynamic

loading than under quasi-static loading, but the Al6061-RAM2 samples exhibited significantly

higher strength and elongation at all strain rates tested. Fractography further confirmed ductile

dimpled fracture in the Al6061-RAM2 samples whereas the Al6061-Sc samples showed cleavage-

like fracture features and limited plastic deformation. The experimental data were also used to

calibrate a modified Johnson-Cook constitutive model for the Al6061-RAM2 material. The

calibrated model captured the increase in yield stress with strain rate. Finally, the finite element





                                                                    iiisimulations in ABAQUS/Explicit provided a reasonable representation of its strain-rate-dependent

tensile response.


Overall, this thesis demonstrates the influence of residual porosity, post-processing, and alloy

modification on the microstructure and strain-rate-dependent mechanical behavior of PBF-LB

Al6061. The  results showed  that  conventional  thermal  post-processing  provided  limited

improvement when residual lack-of-fusion porosity remained significant. On the other hand, the

alloy-modification study revealed that the tensile performance can be significantly improved with

an improvement in printability and a reduction in porosity, as demonstrated with the Al6061-

RAM2 samples. However, the lower performance of the Al6061-Sc samples suggested that alloy

modification alone is not sufficient  if processing conditions or feedstock properties lead to

significant porosity. Together, these findings highlighted porosity as a dominant factor controlling

the mechanical response of PBF-LB Al6061 alloys under quasi-static and dynamic loading and

provided experimental and modelling data for the design of PBF-LB aluminum alloys for

applications involving dynamic or impact loading.

2.3.3.  Mechanical properties


2.3.3.1. Microhardness

Figure 2.13 illustrates the microhardness of the Al6061 specimens measured on the surfaces of the

build and transverse directions. It is observed that direct aging has no evident effect on the hardness

                                      24when compared to the as-built specimen, disagreeing with the results of Zheng et al. [15] for PBF-

LB AlSi10Mg. This is likely due to the low Si content in Al6061, which cannot precipitate

sufficiently after DA to enhance the hardness. However, the as-built and DA specimens still show

the highest hardness values, averaging 81.5 ± 5.7 HV and 82.6 ± 4.8 HV, respectively. In contrast,

a significant decrease in hardness is observed for the T6, annealed, and HIP specimens. The

annealed specimen has hardness values of 60.9 ± 4.2 HV, while the T6 specimen has even lower

values, averaging 53.7 ± 3.4 HV. The decrease in hardness can be attributed to the softening effect

induced by thermal exposure during solution treatment and annealing processes. This reduction in

hardness with increasing temperature is consistent with the thermal softening behavior reported

for as-built PBF-LB Al-Mg-Si alloys [65]. On the other hand, T6 specimen shows slightly higher

hardness than the HIP specimen (49.4 ± 2.81 HV), likely due to partial recovery from subsequent

aging. Lastly, a minor anisotropy in hardness is observed between the two directions, similar to

that reported in previous studies [45,66]. The transverse direction generally shows slightly higher

hardness than the build direction. This difference  is attributed to inherent microstructural

anisotropy that occurs during the PBF-LB process.

comparison, the annealed, T6, and HIP specimens show more closely distributed yield stress values

and greater consistency in mechanical behavior under both quasi-static and dynamic conditions.

This narrower scatter is likely related to residual stress relief during heat treatment, which has been

reported to result in more uniform mechanical behavior for PBF-LB AlSi10Mg in a previous study

[4].

Finally, the apparent elastic modulus of all compression specimens is shown in Figure 2.18b as a

function of strain rate. Based on Hook’s law, the apparent elastic modulus is defined as the ratio

of stress to strain in the elastic range. It is called apparent because the porosity and microstructural

heterogeneity of the AM specimens reduce the measured elastic modulus compared to the nominal

elastic modulus of as-cast Al6061 (69 GPa [52]). In this study, the apparent elastic modulus is

calculated from the slope of the stress-strain curve obtained during uniaxial compression testing

up to 0.001 strain, where the response is approximately linear. For most specimens, the modulus
ranges from approximately 25 to 40 GPa under quasi-static loading (10-4 to 10-3 s-1). DA specimens

generally show the highest modulus, while most HIP specimens have the lowest modulus under

these conditions. This trend is likely explained by the same microstructural factors discussed for

strength reduction earlier, which are residual stress relief, decreasing dislocation density, and the
loss of solid solution strengthening during HIP treatment. At dynamic loading (500 to 1800 s-1),

                                      30the apparent elastic modulus values are between approximately 20 and 35 GPa. However, the data

are more scattered, and no obvious trend is found between the heat treatment conditions.

  a)                          b)





Figure 2.18. (a) Yield stress and (b) elastic modulus of specimens under different strain rates and heat treatment
conditions: As-built, Direct aged, Annealed, T6 (solution treated and artificially aged), and HIP (hot isostatic pressing).


2.3.3.3. Deformation behavior and  strain  field  evolution under  quasi-static and dynamic

compression

In this study, all strain calculations used for stress strain analysis were based on DIC-measured

axial strain, as it provides the direct surface deformation of the specimen. A comparison between

the axial strain obtained from the SHPB wave analysis (Eq. 2.2) and the axial strain measured

directly on the specimen surface using DIC is shown in Figure 2.19. The SHPB-derived strain is

affected by wave interactions at the bar specimen interfaces, impedance mismatch, and cross-

sectional differences. In contrast, DIC strain represents the surface deformation of the specimen

and therefore provides a more direct measurement of the local strain. Because of these interface

effects, the  strain computed from the wave equations  is  slightly  greater  at high  strains.

Nevertheless, both curves follow a similar deformation history.





                                      31Figure 2.19. Comparison of axial strain measured from the SHPB wave analysis (blue) and from DIC on the specimen
surface (red) during dynamic compression.


To evaluate the deformation behavior of the specimens under compression, full-field axial (εxx)

and lateral (εyy) strain distributions generated by DIC were analyzed. Figures 2.20 and 2.21 show

the stress and strain time responses of the specimens in the as-built and post-processed conditions,

along with the corresponding DIC images captured at key points along the loading path under

quasi-static and dynamic loadings, respectively. Image frames labelled 1 to 4 correspond to the

stages marked on the stress-time curve and provide a view of the evolving deformation process.

Under quasi-static loading (see Figure 2.20)  all heat treatment conditions follow a similar

deformation sequence, and the strain maps show an initial elastic stage with minimal gradients

(Frame 1). This is followed by a gradual development of axial and lateral strain heterogeneity as

plastic deformation proceeds (Frames 2-4). Localized regions of higher axial strain (εₓₓ) form and

expand with increasing load. Frame 4 shows that the peak strain regions for axial strain (εₓₓ) are

concentrated at both loading edges, reaching values exceeding 0.20, while for lateral strain (εyy),

the peak strains accumulate in the center of the specimens. The shear strain (εxy) remains negligible

during the test, indicating that the loading is almost pure uniaxial compression without significant

in-plane rotation or bending. Note that none of the specimens show cracking or failure under the

compression tests. Instead, they maintain their structural integrity during testing, and the DIC

pattern is not lost even at peak stress.




                                      32Dynamic loading (see Figure 2.21) reveals that, during the elastic and early plastic stages, the

strain field is roughly uniform across the specimen surface (Frame 1). As the loading continues,

strain gradients emerge, and strain fields evolve smoothly from uniform to local deformation

(frames 2 and 3). The peak axial strain regions (εxx) reach values exceeding 0.20 before unloading

(frame 4), generally concentrated at the center towards the corners of the specimens. Lateral strains

(εyy) remain relatively low, reaching an average of 0.10, and show similar strain concentration from

the center to the corners. Similar to the quasi-static tests (see Figure 2.20), the shear component

(εₓᵧ) stays small during the tests, and no specimens fracture or lose the speckle pattern. Lastly, no

significant or systematic differences are observed between heat treatment conditions in terms of

how strain localizes or propagates through the specimens.

                                      352.4.  Conclusion

In this study, the microstructure and dynamic mechanical properties of PBF-LB processed Al6061

alloy specimens were investigated under various conditions such as as-built, direct aging,

annealing, T6 and hot isostatic pressing. The results showed that the as-built specimen exhibited

measurable porosity (3.66 ± 0.64%) with irregular lack-of-fusion defects and micro-cracks. These

defects were distributed throughout the build volume and were mostly rounded pore morphologies.

Among all heat treatment conditions, porosity values were in the range of ~3.5-5%, indicating that

heat treatments did not completely remove porosity. EBSD analysis also showed that there was no

difference in grain size and texture between heat treatment conditions, indicating that post-

processing had minimal influence on both porosity and texture under the conditions studied here.

In addition, microhardness tests demonstrated that the as-built and DA specimens had the highest

hardness values of 81.5 ± 5.7 HV and 82.6 ± 4.8 HV, respectively. However, annealed, T6 and HIP

conditions softened the material, and HIP specimens had the lowest hardness (49.4 ± 2.8 HV). A

similar trend was observed for flow stress. DA specimens reached the highest flow stress of 348 ±

17 MPa (measured under dynamic loading at 15% plastic strain), and this was followed by as-built

specimens with 333 ± 6 MPa. In contrast, HIP and T6 specimens had the lowest flow stresses with

231 ± 5 MPa and 238 ± 9 MPa, respectively.

P. Ponnusamy, S. Masood, D. Ruan, S. Palanisamy, R. A. Rashid Rahman, and M. A. Kariem. High strain rate behaviour at high temperature of alsi12 parts produced by selective laser melting. IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering, 377:012167, Jun 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899x/377/1/012167, doi:10.1088/1757-899x/377/1/012167. This article has 10 citations.

This excerpt provides details for Ponnusamy et al. (2018), concerning selective-laser-melted (laser-powder-bed-fused) AlSi12 under compression. Cylindrical specimens were built horizontally on the SLM plate, then machined to 8 mm diameter × 8 mm height, giving an aspect ratio of 1.0. Quasi-static tests used a strain rate of 2 × 10^-3 s^-1; room-temperature SHPB tests reached 750 s^-1, while tests at 200 °C reached 1500 s^-1. The 200 °C condition was produced by heating only the specimen immediately before impact; the SHPB incident, transmission, and striker bars remained at room temperature. Thus, this is an initial specimen-temperature condition, not post-build heat treatment. At room temperature, the study reported a negative strain-rate effect, attributed to micro-cracks and adiabatic thermal softening. At 200 °C, it reported a positive strain-rate effect, associated with a rate-controlling thermally activated diffusion mechanism and possible dynamic recrystallization. The excerpt contains no information on a 2020 Ponnusamy study, 400 °C testing, post-build heat treatments, numerical simulations/effects, or comparative build orientations beyond stating that the specimens were built horizontally. It therefore cannot establish those requested details or distinguish additional thermal histories.

## 1. yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 25-29 (Context ID: pqac-00000018)

were analyzed using EBSD. EBSD data were acquired over areas of 350 × 300 µm² using an

acceleration voltage of 20 kV and a step size of 1.25 µm. Furthermore, the density of the specimens

was measured using the Archimedes method. For each condition, five specimens were measured,

and each specimen was tested five times. The theoretical density of Al6061 was taken as 2.70
g/cm3 [52]. In addition, density measurements were verified and porosity was analyzed using X-


                                        11ray microscopy (XRM), which has also been applied to assess porosity changes after HIP in AM

alloys [53]. XRM scanning was performed on a Zeiss Xradia 620 Versa system with an 8 μm

resolution. The XRM data were reconstructed and analyzed using the Dragonfly software. Lastly,

phase analysis was conducted using XRD (Bruker D8 Discover) operated at 40 kV and 40 mA.

Measurements were performed in the 2θ range of 20°-100° at a scanning speed of 2°/min, using

Cu-Kα radiation.


2.2.4.  Mechanical testing


2.2.4.1. Microhardness testing

Microhardness measurements were performed using a Wilson VH1102 microhardness tester.

Before testing, the specimens were ground using SiC abrasive papers down to a 1500-grit finish.

Two surfaces, corresponding to the build direction and transverse direction (see Figure 2.3a), were

tested under a load of 300 gf and a dwell time of 10 seconds. At least ten measurements were made

on each surface of each specimen.


2.2.4.2. Quasi-static testing

Cuboidal compression specimens were used for testing because their flat surfaces provide clear

visibility for high-speed imaging and allow accurate visualization of deformation features using

DIC. The specimens were fabricated with the loading axis perpendicular to the build direction as

shown in Figure 2.3a. This horizontal build orientation was chosen because it is widely reported

to provide the highest strength in metallic parts produced via PBF-LB [37]. Compression tests

were conducted using a Material Test System (MTS 810). Strain measurements were obtained

using the digital image correlation (DIC) method and analyzed in the VIC-2D 6 software using a

subset size of 29 and a step size of 7 pixels, with incremental correlation and the zero-normalized

sum of squared differences (ZNSSD) criterion. To capture the strain fields by the DIC technique,

a high-contrast speckle pattern (Fig. 2.3c) with an average speckle size of approximately 40 µm

was sprayed onto the specimen surfaces using an airbrush. These tests were performed at nominal
strain rates of 0.001 s-1 and 0.0001 s-1, and at least three experiments were conducted for each

condition to verify repeatability.



                                      12    a)                        b)                 c)





Figure 2.3. (a) Dimensions of the cubic specimen for compression testing with build and load orientations (all
dimensions are in millimeters). (b) Example of a fabricated specimen. (c) Example of a specimen sprayed with a
speckle pattern for DIC measurement.


2.2.4.3. Dynamic testing

Dynamic compression tests were performed using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) system.

The system consists of an incident bar, transmitter bar, striker, gas gun, strain gauges, data

acquisition system (DAQ), high-speed camera and gas tank, as shown in Figure 2.4. The bars and

striker are made of hardened maraging steel (Service Steel America C-350) with a diameter of 12.7

mm. The incident and transmitter bars are each 1 m in length, while the striker bar is 300 mm. For

testing, specimens were placed between the incident and transmitter bars, and the striker was

launched using a gas gun to impact the incident bar, creating a compressive stress wave. Strain

waves were measured using strain gauges mounted on the incident and transmitter bars. The

This chapter addresses the thesis objective of understanding how alloy modifications affect the

microstructure, porosity, and strain-rate-dependent mechanical response of PBF-LB Al6061, with

particular focus on Goal 4 outlined in Section 1.3. Sc- and RAM2-modified alloys are investigated

under quasi-static and dynamic tensile loading, and their mechanical responses are examined in

relation to their microstructural features, porosity, and fracture characteristics. The experimental

results also provide the basis for the constitutive modelling presented in Appendix A, which

addresses Goal 5.

modified Al6061 alloys fabricated by laser-beam powder bed fusion,” (2026).

                                      37ABSTRACT

Al6061 is challenging to process by laser-beam powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) because porosity

and cracking formed during the process can reduce its mechanical performance. Various alloy

modification strategies have been developed to address this problem. In the present study, the

influence of Sc and ceramic reinforcement modifications on the microstructure and strain-rate-

dependent tensile response of PBF-LB-processed Al6061 was investigated. Specifically, the study

focuses on PBF-LB of two Al6061 alloys: Al6061-Sc (Sc-modified Al6061 via mechanical

mixing) and Al6061-RAM2 (Al6061 containing 2 vol% of inoculant particles of Ti/B4C). The

Al6061-Sc alloy was fabricated using process parameters selected from a previous process-

optimization  study, whereas  the Al6061-RAM2  alloy was  fabricated using manufacturer-

recommended parameters. The microstructural analysis showed clear differences between the two

modified alloys. The Al6061-RAM2 material had lower porosity (0.28 ± 0.18%) and finer

equiaxed grains, while the Al6061-Sc material exhibited a coarser grain structure and higher
porosity (4.92 ± 0.82%). Tensile properties were evaluated under both quasi-static (10-4-10-2 s-1)
and dynamic (6 × 102-2.8 × 103 s-1) loading conditions using a material testing system and a tensile

split-Hopkinson pressure bar (T-SHPB). At every strain rate investigated, the Al6061-RAM2

material achieved higher strength and ductility than the Al6061-Sc material. In addition, both

materials showed higher ultimate tensile strengths under dynamic loading than under quasi-static

loading. The significant difference in tensile performance between the two modified alloys is

consistent with the substantial difference in porosity. These findings underline the important role

of porosity in governing the tensile response of the modified Al6061 alloys investigated in this

study.


Keywords: Laser-beam powder bed fusion, Modified Al6061, Dynamic tensile behavior, Porosity





                                      383.1.  Introduction

Aluminum alloys are used in automotive, aerospace, defence and general engineering fields owing

to their low density, high mechanical properties and excellent processing performance [2,45]. For

decades, aluminum components have been fabricated through conventional processes such as

casting, forging, and powder metallurgy [71]. In recent years, fusion-based additive manufacturing

(AM) processes such as laser-beam powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) have gained attention to produce

aluminum alloys because they have unique advantages such as design freedom, rapid prototyping,

and reduced material waste [9,11]. Although PBF-LB can have higher manufacturing costs than

conventional processes, eliminating the need for molds and dies can contribute to its economic

competitiveness for low-volume production of complex metal components [72,73]. Nevertheless,

processing aluminum alloys by PBF-LB has some problems such as hot cracking, anisotropy, and

porosity [74]. Porosity formation is a major problem in PBF-LB aluminum alloys because their

high reflectivity and high thermal conductivity can make stable and complete melting difficult

[10,12]. Depending on the processing conditions, insufficient or excessive energy input can lead

to  lack-of-fusion  or  vaporization/keyhole-related  pores,  respectively  [75,76]. Al6061,  an

aluminum alloy widely used in aerospace and automotive applications due to  its strength,

toughness and weldability, is particularly susceptible to solidification defects and exhibits lower

mechanical properties compared to its wrought counterparts [12,68,77].

One effective method to improve the printability of aluminum alloys is microalloying. This method

is implemented by adding alloying elements such as scandium (Sc), zirconium (Zr), and erbium

(Er) into Al  alloys, which refines the microstructure, reduces hot cracking and improves
mechanical properties [21,23,78]. The most well-known example is Scalmalloy®, an Al-Mg-Sc-Zr

alloy  developed  specifically  for AM  [79].  Studies  have shown  that PBF-LB-processed
Scalmalloy® in the as-built condition has an ultimate tensile strength of ~430 MPa at ~20%

elongation [80,81]. Other Sc- and Zr-modified alloys such as Al-Mn-Sc [82], Al-Cu-Sc-Zr [83]

and Al-Mg-Si-Sc-Zr [84] have shown that microalloying can reduce cracking susceptibility and

improve mechanical performance. In line with these findings, the effects of Sc and Zr additions on

the processability and properties of Al6061 in PBF-LB have been investigated [13]. The results

showed that the addition of Zr resulted in the formation of Al3Zr particles, which refined the grains,

suppressed  solidification  cracking, and reduced  porosity.  In  their  study, Zhu  et  al.  [85]


                                      39demonstrated that Sc- and Zr-modified Al6061 fabricated by PBF-LB exhibited 99.92% relative

density with an ultimate tensile strength of ~330 MPa at ~21% elongation in the as-built condition.

In parallel, alternative reinforcement methods such as ceramic-modified Al6061 feedstock known

as Al6061-RAM2 containing B4C and Ti particles have been investigated [22,24]. In their study,

Rosito et al. [22] reported that PBF-LB-processed Al6061-RAM2 reached an ultimate tensile

strength of ~260 MPa, which is higher than the ~60-90 MPa reported for unmodified Al6061 in

the literature [45,86,87].

Potential applications for PBF-LB aluminum alloys include instrument and antenna brackets in

aerospace applications and structural brackets in the automotive ind

PBF-LB Al6061 components subjected to impact or high-rate loading conditions.

available gas-atomized Al6061-RAM2 powder (Elementum 3D, USA) produced by Reactive

0.3 wt.% Sc powder (Stanford Advanced Materials, California, USA) with gas-atomized Al6061

powder (Valimet Inc., California, USA) using a planetary high-energy ball milling machine

(Pulverisette 5, Fritsch GmbH, Germany) at 150 rpm for 120 minutes. The morphology of the

parameters provided by Elementum 3D were used: 370 W laser power, 1086 mm/s scanning speed,

Before microstructural characterization, samples were prepared following the ASTM E3-11(2017)

metallographic sample preparation standard [51] by sequential grinding and polishing, followed

by final polishing with a 0.05 μm colloidal silica suspension. Microstructural characterization was

performed using electron backscatter diffraction attached to a field-emission scanning electron

microscope (FE-SEM, Zeiss Sigma). Grain orientation, grain size distribution, and texture were

evaluated from the EBSD data. The scans were conducted at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV.
Scan areas of 70 × 70 μm2 and 300 × 350 μm2 were used for the Al6061-RAM2 and Al6061-Sc

samples, respectively, with step sizes of 0.2 μm for Al6061-RAM2 and 1 μm for Al6061-Sc. The

reported mean grain size and standard deviation were calculated from all individual grains

identified within each analyzed EBSD map. Porosity characterization was additionally carried out

using X-ray microscopy. The scans were performed using a Zeiss Xradia 620 Versa system with a

spatial resolution of 7 μm. Reconstruction and quantitative pore analysis of the acquired datasets

were conducted using Dragonfly software. Pores were segmented by manually selecting a

grayscale threshold for each XRM dataset based on visual agreement between the segmented

regions and the pore features observed in the reconstructed images. To evaluate the sensitivity of

the calculated porosity to threshold selection, the analysis was repeated using threshold values 5%

below and 5% above the selected value. The mean and standard deviation of the porosity values

obtained from the three threshold settings were reported as an indication of segmentation

sensitivity.

After tensile testing, fracture morphologies were analyzed using a field-emission scanning electron

3.3.   Results and discussion

3.3.1.  Microstructure

X-ray microscopy results of the Al6061-Sc (Fig. 3.5a) and Al6061-RAM2 (Fig. 3.5b) samples are

presented, including pore volume distributions, cumulative pore volume fractions, and 3D pore

reconstructions. The Al6061-RAM2 sample exhibits a porosity level of 0.28 ± 0.18%, while the

Al6061-Sc material shows a significantly higher porosity of 4.92 ± 0.82%. The corresponding

relative density of the Al6061-RAM2 sample (~99.72%) is comparable to values reported for PBF-

LB-processed Al6061-RAM2C (>99.7%) [96]. In contrast, the relative density of the Al6061-Sc


                                      45sample (~95.08%) is significantly lower than the 99.98% relative density reported for Sc-modified

Al6061 fabricated by PBF-LB [46]. One possible contributing factor to this difference is the

feedstock preparation method. The Al6061-Sc powder used in the present study was produced by

mechanically mixing Sc powder with gas-atomized Al6061 powder, whereas pre-alloyed atomized

powder was used in the literature study [46]. Differences in processing parameters may also have

contributed to the difference in relative density. Moreover, pore volume distributions show that
most pores in both materials are within the 103-105 µm3 range. However, the Al6061-Sc material
has a dominant interconnected pore cluster in the 108-109 µm3 range, which is nearly 80% of the

total pore volume. This interconnected defect likely reduces the effective load-bearing area and

leads  to premature  fracture  in  the Al6061-Sc  material. The  irregular and interconnected

morphology of this pore cluster is consistent with lack-of-fusion-type defects forming due to

insufficient melting and poor interlayer bonding [12,76]. In contrast, the smaller and more isolated

pores in Al6061-RAM2 indicate that a more complete densification occurred under the processing

conditions used. However, because the two materials were produced using different feedstocks and

PBF-LB  processing  parameters,  the  difference  in  porosity cannot be  attributed  to  alloy

modification alone.

81.5 ± 5.7 HV was reported for as-built PBF-LB Al6061 [97]. The higher microhardness observed

Therefore, the lower density in Al6061-Sc is likely due to the significantly higher pore volume

3.3.2.2. Quasi-static and dynamic tensile behavior

Figure 3.7a shows representative engineering stress-strain curves of the Al6061-RAM2 samples,

while Figure 3.7b shows the corresponding curves for all tested Al6061-Sc samples under quasi-

static and dynamic tensile loading. For each testing condition, three samples were tested, and good

repeatability was observed among the Al6061-RAM2 tests. The measured yield stress, ultimate

tensile strength (UTS), and elongation values are summarized in Table 3.1 together with literature

data for other additively manufactured aluminum alloys for comparison. The Al6061-RAM2

samples demonstrate significantly higher tensile stress and ductility than the Al6061-Sc samples

under all tested strain rates. Under quasi-static loading, the Al6061-RAM2 samples reach ultimate
tensile strengths of 208 ± 5 MPa and 209 ± 4 MPa at strain rates of 10-3 s-1 and 10-2 s-1, respectively,

with elongation values of 8.2 ± 1.8% and 7.9 ± 1.1%, respectively. These values are comparable

to previously reported Al6061 RAM systems in the literature, where ultimate tensile strengths of

256 ± 11 MPa [22] and 235 ± 1 MPa [96] were reported. In contrast, the Al6061-Sc samples show

significantly lower mechanical performance, exhibiting a quasi-static ultimate tensile strength of

12 ± 7 MPa and an elongation of 0.2 ± 0.1%. This value is significantly lower than that reported

for another Sc-modified PBF-LB Al6061 alloy in the literature, where the ultimate tensile strength

reached 350 MPa [46].

                                      48Furthermore, under dynamic loading, both materials show higher ultimate tensile strengths

compared with quasi-static loading. The Al6061-RAM2 samples reach an ultimate tensile strength
of 233 ± 3 MPa and 239 ± 3 MPa at strain rates of 2.1 × 103 s-1 and 2.7 × 103 s-1, respectively,

while maintaining elongation values above 19%. In contrast, the Al6061-Sc samples reach an

ultimate tensile strength of 33 ± 8 MPa with an elongation of 0.5 ± 0.1% under dynamic loading.
It should be noted that, except for the 1.5 × 103 s-1 condition, all Al6061-RAM2 samples tested
under dynamic loading fractured during the first loading wave. Although the 1.5 × 103 s-1 samples

also fractured after testing, failure did not occur within the first loading pulse due to insufficient

loading duration related to the striker length at this strain rate.

Overall, the Al6061-RAM2 samples demonstrate more stable tensile deformation and higher

strength under both quasi-static and dynamic conditions, while the Al6061-Sc samples show

premature fracture and substantially lower strength. The difference between the two materials is

consistent with the microstructural observations discussed earlier. The Al6061-RAM2 material

contains a finer equiaxed grain structure and lower porosity, which contribute to its higher load-

bearing capacity. In contrast, the Al6061-Sc material contains significantly higher porosity,

including a large pore cluster, which likely reduces the effective load-bearing area and promotes

failure. The significantly lower mechanical properties observed in the Al6061-Sc samples

compared with previously reported Sc-modified PBF-LB Al6061 [46], together with the observed

interconnected pore cluster and premature fracture, indicate that severe porosity likely plays a

major role in their lower tensile performance and may limit the strengthening benefits of Sc

addition. Lastly, the Al6061-RAM2 samples exhibit mechanical properties comparable to several

previously reported reinforced Al6061 alloys, whereas the Al6061-Sc samples demonstrate

significantly lower tensile performance than most of the PBF-LB Al6061 alloys summarized in

<jats:p>We uniaxially and shocklessly compressed an additively manufactured aluminum alloy, laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) AlSi10Mg, to peak stresses ranging from 4.4 to 14.8 GPa at peak strain rates on the order of 106s−1 via a series of magnetic loading experiments to measure the principal isentrope, yield strength, and shear modulus as a function of material orientation and applied stress. We did not observe significant anisotropy in any of the measured quantities. We found that the principal isentrope, within the uncertainty and up to our peak stress, overlaps the material’s Hugoniot. We measured yield strengths and shear moduli ranging from 0.28 to 0.81 GPa and 36 to 52 GPa, respectively. Our results indicate that LPBF AlSi10Mg behaves similarly to wrought Al alloys under quasi-isentropic compression.</jats:p>

  A novel laser powder bed fusion Al-Fe-Zr alloy for superior
                 strength-conductivity trade-off

    Camille Pauzona,*, Maxence Buttarda, Arthur Desprésa, Béchir Chehabb,
                  Jean-Jacques Blandina, Guilhem Martina


aUniversité Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, SIMaP, 38000, Grenoble, France
bConstellium Technology Center, Parc économique Centr’Alp, 38341, Voreppe, France

*Corresponding author : [email redacted]



                         ABSTRACT

New aluminium alloy design strategies for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) are needed to target
high strength and conductivity applications and substitute the traditional 6xxx series which
suffers from hot cracking during LPBF processing. This study presents the route followed to
design a novel Al-Fe-Zr alloy offering good processability, superior yield strength (310 MPa)
and thermal conductivity (180 W/m·K) after direct ageing (400°C/4h). The multi-scale
characterization, combining scanning and transmission electron microscopy with automated
crystallographic  orientation mapping and  energy  dispersive  spectroscopy,  reveals  the
precipitation of plate-like Al13Fe4 and coherent Al3Zr-L12 nanoprecipitates upon ageing,
enhancing the material’s strength. In turn, the associated solid solution depletion results in a
significant conductivity increase. The strategy to select low vapour pressure elements and slow
diffusers in Al, as well as the low solubility of Fe in Al demonstrates the ability through alloy
design for additive manufacturing to fill gaps in the material property space.

Keywords: Additive manufacturing; Laser powder bed fusion; Alloy design; Aluminium
alloys; mechanical performance; electrical conductivity.





                                     1                           Manuscript for Scripta Materialia


      Combining low  density,  high  corrosion  resistance and  desirable  physical and
mechanical properties, Al-alloys are a workhorse of the transport and energy industries. Laser
powder bed fusion (LPBF) offers new perspectives to achieve near-net shape complex
components in few manufacturing steps, compared to the traditional routes of cast and wrought
products.
The preferred approach to produce Al-based LPBF components has been to use casting alloys
[1], for example AlSi7Mg and AlSi10Mg. Unfortunately, these grades do not deliver high
mechanical performance when LPBF-processed [2,3]. Al-alloys from the 6xxx series provide
both good strength and conductivity after a T6 heat-treatment and would be excellent
candidates to manufacture heat exchangers. However, they suffer from hot cracking during
autogenous laser welding because of their large freezing range and coefficient of thermal
expansion [4], and hot cracking also occurs during LPBF [5–8]. Uddin et al.[9] managed to
suppress hot cracking using powder bed heating to 500°C. Despite its success, this approach is
not compatible with industrial LPBF systems. Besides, adjustments to the alloy composition
have been considered, with addition of grain refiners that promote the heterogeneous nucleation
of Al grains, making the alloy more resistant to cracking. These refiners can either be
inoculating agents admixed to the powder like TiB2 and TiC [10,11], or primary phases formed
in situ such as Al3X (X=Zr, Sc) [5,6,8,12]. In this case, the benefit is two-fold with the
additional potential for precipitation strengthening through post-ageing treatment [13,14]. It
has also been suggested to tune the powder composition to favour elements which do not
increase the solidification range [15,16]. These approaches have addressed to some extent the
cracking issues of the 6xxx series. But other challenges remain, connected to laser-induced
solute evaporation and the need for further solutionizing and quenching. Briefly, there is a
necessity to develop novel Al-alloys with strength and conductivity comparable or surpassing
that of the 6xxx series combined with good LPBF processability.
This work introduces a new Al-alloy designed for LPBF to achieve a superior strength –
conductivity trade-off, by leveraging the unique characteristics of the process: the relatively
high solid-liquid interface velocities and high thermal gradients resulting in high cooling rates.
The multiscale characterization reveals unique microstructural features of the Al-Fe-Zr alloy
inherited from LPBF and their evolution upon ageing, further connected to the material tensile
response and conductivity.
     One criterion for alloying element selection is a low vapour pressure in comparison to
common solutes like Zn and Mg, which tend to restrict the processing window to low energy
inputs. The loss of such elements can lead to local composition variations and for example
reduced precipitation hardening for 6xxx or 7xxx alloys. Their vaporization can affect the melt
pool stability, lead to porosity formation, and generated vapours may interact with the laser,
resulting in diminished and varying energy input. These challenges will become more
predominant as production capacities are boosted with high power, multi-laser systems, and
high layer thicknesses [17]. An additional criterion is to favour elements with low diffusivity
in Al to limit the extent of in situ precipitation during thermal cycles and retain a supersaturated
solution in the as-built state. Finally, toxic elements such as Be are avoided as well as certain
Critical Raw Materials (CRMs) like Sc bringing high costs and supply risks.
      With these criteria, Zr and Fe were shortlisted as they combine both low vapour
pressure and low diffusivity in solid Al. Zr plays a dual role with the formation of primary
Al3Zr resulting in grain refinement, limiting hot cracking, and its contribution to precipitation
strengthening through post-ageing treatment [18]. It diffuses in Al more slowly than Sc [19].


                                     2                           Manuscript for Scripta Materialia


Similarly, Fe exhibits a low diffusivity in Al [20]. Fe is of special interest for its very low
equilibrium solubility in Al (0.044 wt.% at 654°C, computed with Thermo-Calc, TCAL6). Its
minor content in the solid solution  is expected to not significantly reduce the matrix
conductivity. In addition, from Scheil-Gulliver calculations, Fe is expected to form Al13Fe4
(Fig. S1). Based on this rationale, gas atomised powder with chemical composition given in

and a 60 µm layer thickness, near-fully-dense samples (> 99.7 %) were manufactured. The
specimens were heat treated for stress-relief at 300°C for 2 hours before baseplate removal.

       It is evident from the information presented in Table 1 that there is a lot of interest in understanding
the SLM processability of various aluminium alloys. Olakanmi et al. [139] reported in detail the
inﬂuence of process parameters, powder properties, and laser types on the densiﬁcation of aluminium
alloys. Moreover, they also reported the potential issues arising during the SLM of aluminium alloys,
such as metallurgical defects, porosity, and oxidation. The primary causes for these processing
challenges include high reﬂectivity, high thermal conductivity, and poor ﬂowability of aluminium
alloy powders, which, as reported by Aversa et al. [140], can be addressed by the development of new
alloys speciﬁcally designed to improve the SLM-printability of various aluminium alloys. This idea
was corroborated by Sercombe and Li [141] who reported improved microstructures and enhanced
mechanical properties of various aluminium metal matrix composites fabricated via SLM.
    The primary research focus areas of most of the published literature on SLM of aluminium
alloys can be broadly classiﬁed into four categories, viz, process parameter optimization, eﬀects of
build orientation, in-situ and post heat treatment strategies, and modelling and numerical analysis of
print-part performance as listed in the overview of publications in Table 2. It is clear from this overview
that AlSi10Mg alloy has received maximum attention of research papers for all four research focus areas
for mechanical properties, with a large number of researchers paying attention to the eﬀects of build
orientation and heat treatment of this alloy. More research needs to be done on process optimization and
eﬀects of the build orientation and heat treatment of AlSi12 alloy and other two less popular A356 and
A357 alloys processed by SLM. As reported by Rometsch et al. [142] and Zhang et al. [143], these studies
aim to improve the performance of SLM-printed aluminium components via: (a) optimizing powder
characteristics, (b) optimizing process parameters to obtain 100% dense parts, (c) minimizing the
defects such as residual stresses, distortion, and cracking, (d) optimizing post heat treatment techniques
to achieve desired mechanical properties, (e) understanding the microstructural characteristics of the
print-part, and (f) anisotropic mechanical properties as a result of varying build orientation.

3. Mechanical Properties of SLM-Printed Aluminium Alloys

     Characterisation of the mechanical properties of any additively manufactured part is generally
very demanding. Although ASTM F3122-14 presents standard guidelines to evaluate most of the
mechanical properties of 3D-printed metallic materials, there is no set standard developed for this
purpose, making it diﬃcult to benchmark and/or compare the properties of the same material printed
using diﬀerent AM printers with varying geometries. Therefore, extensive research has been published
to characterize various types of mechanical properties of SLM processed Al alloys under static,
dynamic, and heat treatment conditions. Table 3 is a compilation of the various mechanical properties
investigated by researchers for four main types of SLM-printed aluminium alloys, namely AlSi10Mg,
AlSi12, A356, and A357.Materials 2020, 13, 4301                                                                                                                                                  31 of 51

     Table 3 shows that maximum research eﬀort has been directed to investigate the tensile properties
of SLM processed aluminium alloys. In most of these publications, eﬀect of build orientation and
heat treatment on microhardness, yield strength (YS) and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) has been
studied. Many of these publications have also discussed the microstructure variation in the samples
arising due to rapid heating and cooling encountered in the SLM process and relate them to the
mechanical property relationships. Table 3 also reveals that some important mechanical properties
such as quasi-static compression, dynamic (high strain rate), fatigue, impact, ﬂexural and wear have
received very little attention of researchers. These properties are of signiﬁcance in many automotive,
aerospace, and biomedical applications.

is discussed below.

3.1. SLM-Printed AlSi10Mg

    AlSi10Mg is one of the most common aluminium alloys and ﬁnds wide applications in various
industries of 3D printing applications such as automotive and aerospace. The eﬀect of build orientations
in horizontal (H), inclined (I), and vertical (V) directions, and the eﬀect of post heat treatment on the
tensile mechanical properties of SLM-printed AlSi10Mg are summarized in Table 4. In most of the
studies, the tensile samples built in horizontal direction on the build plate seem to provide higher
tensile strength than the sample build in vertical direction. In most studies, it was observed that heat
treated (HT) SLM samples display reduced tensile strength and increased ductility than the as-built
(AB) SLM samples. Very few studies have been conducted to assess the eﬀect of build orientation
on heat treated SLM samples. Table 4 also presents results of some studies carried out on fatigue
and fracture toughness of the SLM-built parts. Very few studies have been undertaken on ﬂexural
behaviour of the printed aluminium parts. Table 4 shows results of work carried out on the quasi-static
and dynamic compression of SLM processed aluminium samples. Again, a great deal of studies
are required to understand the quasi-static compression and high strain rate dynamic tensile and
compressive behaviour of SLM-processed aluminium parts for diﬀerent orientations and heat treatment
conditions. Moreover, the mechanical performance of SLM-processed aluminium alloys operating at
elevated temperatures have also not received the attention of researchers.

      Samples were produced with an EOS M290 under Argon. The baseplate made of a
5XXX-serie Al-alloy was preheated to 100°C, and the stripe scanning pattern was rotated by
67° between layers. Using a 370 W power, a 1400 mm/s scan speed, 0.13 mm hatch distance
and a 60 µm layer thickness, near-fully-dense samples (> 99.7 %) were manufactured. The
specimens were heat treated for stress-relief at 300°C for 2 hours before baseplate removal.
Such stress-relief post-processing is commonly applied to LPBF Al components to avoid
unwanted deformation, see e.g. [21,22]. Samples were then subjected to a post-fabrication
ageing treatment at 400°C for 4 hours, identified as the peak ageing with 110 ± 2 HV, vs. 65 ±
2 HV after stress-relief. The low diffusivity of Zr in the matrix explains the high ageing
temperature.
Microstructure characterization was performed using a scanning electron microscope (Zeiss
Gemini SEM 500 FEG) equipped with an electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detector.
The samples were polished until a 1µm diamond suspension step, and a final vibratory
polishing. EBSD maps were acquired with a 0.3 µm step size at 20 kV. High angle grain
boundaries plotted in black on the orientation maps are defined by a misorientation >10°. The
MATLAB toolbox MTex was used to compute the grain sphericity defined as the ratio of the
grain area to the product of the perimeter and equivalent radius (equal to 0.5 for a perfect
circle).
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was conducted with a TEM FEG JEOL 2100 and
perform energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) by operating at 200 kV. Thin foils were

were retrieved using ACOM (Automated Crystallographic Orientation Mapping) with the

    Strain rate sensitivity of the
   aluminium-magnesium-scandium alloy - Scalmalloy®


     Puneeth Jakkula1,∗, Georg Ganzenmüller1,2,∗∗, Florian Gutmann2, and Stefan Hiermaier1,2

      1Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg, Sustainable Systems Engineering – INATECH, Emmy-Noether-

      2Fraunhofer Institute for High-Speed Dynamics, Ernst-Mach-Institut – EMI, Ernst-Zermelo-Straße 4,

                Abstract. This work investigates the strain rate sensitivity of the aluminium-
               magnesium-scandium alloy Scalmalloy, which is used extensively for additive
                 manufacturing of lightweight structures. This high strength aluminium alloy
                combines very good weldability, machinability and mechanical strength: it can
                be heat-treated to reach nominal ultimate tensile strengths in excess of 500 MPa.
           We report tensile tests at strain rates ranging from 10−3 /s to 103 /s at room tem-
                   perature.  It is well known that Al-Mg alloys exhibit a negative strain rate de-
                pendency in combination with serrated ﬂow caused by the Portevin-Le Chatelier
                  eﬀect, which describes the interaction of Mg solutes with dislocation propaga-
                    tions. In contrast, in Al-Sc alloys, the ﬂow stress increases with increasing strain
                    rate and displays positive strain rate dependency. Additionally, the presence of
               Sc in the form of Al3-Sc provides a ﬁne-grained microstructure which allows
                 higher tensile and fatigue strength. This research shows how these combined
                 eﬀects interact in the case of Scalmalloy, which contains both Mg and Sc. Tests
                  are performed at quasi-static, intermediate and high strain rates with a servo-
                  hydraulic testing machine and a Split-Hopkinson tension bar. Local specimen
                    strain was performed using 2D Digital Image Correlation.



    1 Introduction

      Selective Laser Melting (SLM) of metal structures in Additive manufacturing (AM) has the
       ability to manufacture complex geometries without special tooling. This favours the produc-
      tion of lightweight, high strength materials which are increasingly utilised in various ﬁelds
      of automotive and aircraft industry [1–4]. The dynamic loading due to crash and impact are
      frequently encountered in these applications. It is therefore a necessity to know the strain-rate
     dependency of the material to quantify crashworthiness.
         This work studies the Scandium modiﬁed Aluminium-Magnesium alloy AA5028 which
     has been developed and patented by APworks and sold under the trade name Scalmalloy.
     According to the manufacturer, it is based on the AA5xxx series Al-Mg alloys with an Mg
      content of 3.2 - 4.8 wt.-% and Sc 0.02 - 0.04 wt.-% [5]. The addition of Scandium improves
      the strength, weldability and corrosion resistance [6]. The yield stress of the as-built ma-
       terial is approximately 350 MPa which can be increased by heat-treating to approximately

     550 MPa [5].  These numbers, combined with the low mass density of 2.7 g/cm3, make
     Scalmalloy an interesting candidate for lightweight crash-absorbing structures. Its strain-rate
       sensitivity, however, is diﬃcult to predict. Al-Sc alloys exhibit positive strain rate sensitivity
     with increased yield stress at elevated strain rates [7]. In contrast, Al-Mg alloys are known
      to exhibit negative strain rate sensitivity, at least up to moderate strain rates of 103 /s [8]. To
     answer the question on how these eﬀects combine in Scalmalloy, we study its dynamic be-
      haviour at four diﬀerent strain rates ranging from 10−3 /s to 1000 /s using servo-hydraulic and
      split-Hopkinson testing methods. Both as-built (non-heat-treated) and heat-treated specimens
      are investigated, and the resulting data is analysed in terms of the strain-rate dependency of
      Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) and strain at failure.


    2 Material and methods

      2.1 Scalmalloy

   A commercial Laser Beam Melting system (EOS M400) equipped with a 1 kW laser unit
      (YLR-series, Continuous Wave (CW)-laser, wavelength 1070 nm) produced a total of 60
     specimens from a single feedstock with dimensions of  20 × 120 mm2. The specimens were
      printed in a 90 degree orientation to the build plate. Building platform heated to 40°C acted as
      the base to print the specimens in layers of 60 µm. According to APworks recommendation,
      half of the batch was heat treated for 4 hours at 325°C. The specimen geometry shown in
      Figure 1 was CNC milled to dimensions. This geometry is chosen because it serves well with
      the constraints of our split-Hopkinson tension bar.





      Figure 1. Specimen geometry with cylindrical gauge region of  4 × 15. All dimensions are in mm.


      2.2 Quasi static tensile testing

     The quasi static tensile tests were performed on the machine Instron 8801 system with 50 kN
      load cell at room temperature. The cross-head velocities of the machine are chosen to achieve
       strain rates of 0.001 /s, 0.1 /s and 10 /s. Nominal specimen strain was calculated using 2D
      Digital Image Correlation (DIC) with the commercial code GOM correlate software, with a
      resolution of 1 pixel = 0.026 mm. An airbrush gun is used to create a ﬁne speckle pattern with
     an approximate speckle size of 0.1 mm. High speed camera (Photron SAZ) with 1024 × 1024
      resolution recorded the deformation images. A virtual extensometer (on 2D DIC images)
     was deﬁned over the parallel gauge region to calculate the nominal strain. The nominal
       strain could be evaluated up to the point of failure. From prior experience, the accuracy
      of the nominal strain measurement is better than 2% of the indicated value. Additionally,
    we evaluated the local strain in the necking region.  This, however, was only possible for
      small local strains, as DIC then failed to correctly track deformation ﬁeld. The beginning of

     103 /s. Figure 2 shows the conﬁguration of SHTB apparatus. Compared to other SHTBs, this

     and output bars are 16 mm diameter aluminium rods. The striker is a hollow aluminium tube
      of 40 mm outer diameter and 20 mm inner diameter. Strain gauge 1 on the input bar and strain
     gauge 2 on output bar measure the incident wave, εinc, and transmitted wave, εtra respectively.
     Force is measured via strain gauges on the bars, connected diagonally in a Wheatstone bridge
       circuit to eliminate bending information. The Wheatstone bridge circuit is driven in constant
      voltage mode and its output is increased by a factor of 100 using an ampliﬁer. This signal is
      recorded by a data acquisition (DAQ) card operating at 10 MHz and 16 bit resolution. The
      conversion factor from strain to force is established via a calibration procedure by placing a
      force censor between input and output bars, a static load is applied onto the bars. More details
     on the setup is described in [9]. Similar to that of quasi-static experiments the specimens are
      speckled with white and black spray paint with speckle resolution of 1 pixel = 0.067 mm.

     manner as that of the low strain rate experiments.

    3 Results and discussion

      3.1 Tensile tests results

     The nominal stress-strain curves are shown in Figure 3 for as-built and heat treated specimens.
     At strain rate 10−3 /s, obvious serrations in the curves are visible for as-built specimens. These
      are presumably due to the Portevin-Le-Chatelier (PLC) eﬀect, which describes the locking of
     a moving dislocation due to solute Mg atoms [8]. At higher strain rates, this eﬀect diminishes
      as the diﬀusion speed of solute Mg becomes slow compared to the dislocation speed.
        The characteristic properties like ultimate tensile strength σmax, strain at failure εf , yield
      strength and necking strain are reported in Table 1. Note that the value of the strain rate at
      yield is uncertain for the SHTB experiment as yielding occurs during the rise of the load-
      ing pulse. Our quasi-static data is in agreement with prior work on Scalmalloy [10], where
     an Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) of 334 MPa and 540 MPa was reported for as-built and
      heat-treated specimens, respectively. The failure behaviour is brittle for the heat-treated spec-
      imens, with almost no necking. Whereas, as-built specimens exhibit limited necking with
      diameter at the failure location of 75% to the initial value.
