Ageing a specimen before a room-temperature test is a different experiment. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000062)

The verified experiments are summarized below. “Temperature” means the specimen’s temperature *during loading*, unless explicitly identified as a prior treatment. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000063)

| Alloy / source | Loading and strain rate | Test temperature vs. post-treatment | Main result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Scalmalloy — Jakkula et al. (2021)** | Split-Hopkinson **tension** at **1000 ± 100 s⁻¹**; servo-hydraulic tests at 0.001–10 s⁻¹ | All tests at **room temperature**. As-built specimens were compared with specimens aged at **325 °C for 4 h** before testing; this was not elevated-temperature testing. | At 1000 s⁻¹, as-built UTS was **342.5 ± 1.6 MPa** with **29.5 ± 0.4%** failure strain; aged UTS was **497.0 ± 3.0 MPa** with **15.0 ± 2.2%** failure strain. UTS showed weak negative rate sensitivity, while failure strain increased at high rate. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) |
| **AlSi12 — Ponnusamy et al. (2018)** | Split-Hopkinson **compression**: maximum **750 s⁻¹** at room temperature and **1500 s⁻¹** at 200 °C; quasi-static comparator at 0.002 s⁻¹ | Specimens were initially at either **room temperature or 200 °C**. For hot SHPB tests, only the specimen was heated; the bars remained at room temperature. No post-build heat treatment was investigated. | A **negative** strain-rate effect was observed at room temperature and a **positive** effect at 200 °C. Stress–strain curves were presented, but reliable numerical flow stresses were not tabulated. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000015) |
| **Unmodified Al6061 — Yilmaz et al. (2026)** | Split-Hopkinson **compression** at **500–800** and **1500–1800 s⁻¹**; quasi-static tests at 0.0001 and 0.001 s⁻¹ | Tests were at **room temperature**. As-built, direct-aged (DA), annealed (AN), T6, and HIP conditions were compared; these were prior post-treatments, not elevated test temperatures. | Flow stress at 15% plastic strain and 1500–1800 s⁻¹: as-built **333 ± 6 MPa**; DA **348 ± 17 MPa**; AN **246 ± 6 MPa**; T6 **238 ± 9 MPa**; HIP **231 ± 5 MPa**. Every condition showed positive rate sensitivity. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000062) |
| **Al6061–0.3 wt.% Sc — Yilmaz (2026 thesis)** | Split-Hopkinson **tension** at approximately **600 s⁻¹**; premature fracture prevented higher rates | **Room-temperature** tests on as-built specimens; no test-temperature variation | At 600 s⁻¹, UTS was **33 ± 8 MPa** and failure elongation was **0.5 ± 0.1%**. Severe porosity of approximately 4.92% and an interconnected pore cluster dominated the poor response. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023) |
| **Al6061–RAM2 with 2 vol.% Ti/B₄C inoculants — Yilmaz (2026 thesis)** | Split-Hopkinson **tension** at approximately **1500–2700 s⁻¹** | **Room-temperature** tests on as-built specimens; no test-temperature variation | At 2700 s⁻¹, yield stress was **192 ± 1 MPa**, UTS was **239 ± 3 MPa**, and elongation was **21.0 ± 2.0%**. UTS rose from approximately 208–209 MPa quasi-statically to 239 MPa dynamically. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023) |


*Table: Verified high-strain-rate tensile and compression measurements on LPBF aluminum alloys other than AlSi10Mg. The table distinguishes elevated specimen test temperature from post-build thermal treatment.*

### What the measurements show

- **Scalmalloy (AA5028):** Jakkula and colleagues used an EOS laser-powder-bed system and a split-Hopkinson **tension** bar. Their 2021 conference report and journal paper describe the same experimental programme, not two independent datasets: tests at approximately **1,000 s⁻¹**, with lower-rate comparators, on as-built and **325 °C/4 h pre-aged** material. At the high rate, the as-built and pre-aged ultimate tensile strengths were **342.5 ± 1.6** and **497.0 ± 3.0 MPa**, respectively; failure strains were **29.5 ± 0.4%** and **15.0 ± 2.2%**. All mechanical tests were at **room temperature**. Ultimate strength declined weakly as rate increased, whereas failure strain increased at the highest rate. The authors explicitly caution that their tests cannot disentangle intrinsic rate effects from adiabatic heating and call for experiments that vary *test* temperature at fixed rate. Their target 1,000 s⁻¹ rate was reached **after yield**, an important qualification when interpreting the reported yield stresses. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000058)

- **AlSi12:** Ponnusamy and colleagues’ 2018 paper reports split-Hopkinson **compression** of horizontally built SLM cylinders, compared with quasi-static compression at the same specimen temperatures. Maximum dynamic rates were **750 s⁻¹ at room temperature** and **1,500 s⁻¹ at 200 °C**. For the hot test, they heated the **specimen**, leaving the bars at room temperature. They report a *negative* apparent rate effect at room temperature but a *positive* one at 200 °C; their stress–strain plots display those comparisons. Because the two dynamic temperature conditions also used **different maximum rates**, this is evidence of temperature-dependent high-rate response, **not** an isolated measurement of temperature dependence at one fixed high rate. A later paper entitled *Dynamic compressive behaviour of selective laser melted AlSi12 alloy: Effect of elevated temperature and heat treatment* (Ponnusamy et al., *Additive Manufacturing* **36**, 101614, 2020; DOI **10.1016/j.addma.2020.101614**) is another directly relevant lead, but its full text could not be verified here; no additional test temperatures or numerical outcomes are attributed to it. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057)

- **Al6061:** Yilmaz and colleagues’ published study, *Mechanical behavior of Al6061 produced by laser powder bed fusion: Effects of heat treatments and strain rates* (*Materials Science and Engineering A* **950**, 149574, 2026; DOI **10.1016/j.msea.2025.149574**), is reproduced as a chapter of Yilmaz’s accessible 2026 thesis. It reports split-Hopkinson **compression at 500–800 and 1,500–1,800 s⁻¹**. At 15% plastic strain and the higher rate, flow stress was **333 ± 6 MPa as-built**, **348 ± 17 MPa direct-aged**, **246 ± 6 MPa annealed**, **238 ± 9 MPa T6**, and **231 ± 5 MPa after HIP**. Each condition had a higher flow stress under dynamic than quasi-static loading. These are comparisons of **prior thermal treatments at room-temperature test conditions**, not high-rate tests performed at the heat-treatment temperatures. The material retained approximately **3.5–5% porosity**, limiting generalization to denser LPBF Al6061. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063)

- **Modified Al6061:** A separate chapter of that thesis, described there as **submitted for publication**, reports room-temperature split-Hopkinson **tension** on LPBF Al6061 mixed with **0.3 wt% Sc** and on ceramic-inoculated **Al6061–RAM2**. The Sc material reached about **600 s⁻¹**, with **33 ± 8 MPa** ultimate strength and **0.5 ± 0.1%** elongation; severe interconnected porosity caused premature fracture. RAM2 reached **2,700 s⁻¹**, with **239 ± 3 MPa** ultimate strength and **21.0 ± 2.0%** elongation. These formulations are **not Scalmalloy or A205/A20X**, and the thesis does not vary their specimen test temperature. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000059)

### Status of the other named alloys

I did **not identify a verified ≥100 s⁻¹ tensile or compressive test on LPBF A20X/A205, AlSi7Mg (A356/A357), an Al–Ce alloy, or Al–Fe–Zr**. This is a statement about the located literature, **not proof that no unpublished or unindexed measurement exists**. The distinction matters because several close-looking results fail the rate criterion: the LPBF **Al–Fe–Zr** report gives room-temperature tensile properties after **400 °C/4 h ageing**, not high-rate tests; LPBF **Al–Ce** literature reports elevated-temperature tensile strength and thermal exposure, but not a verified qualifying Hopkinson test; and the surveyed A356/A357 literature emphasizes tensile, fatigue and shear properties rather than qualifying high-rate uniaxial measurements. A 2025 LPBF **Al–Fe–Cr–X** study actually varied *test* temperature from room temperature to 400 °C, but its compression strain-rate steps were only **10⁻⁵–10⁻² s⁻¹**. Likewise, LPBF Al–Mn–Cr–Zr was tensile-tested up to 573 K, including a rate comparison reaching **1% s⁻¹ = 0.01 s⁻¹**—far below 100 s⁻¹. (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000051)

**Bottom line:** For the specific combination of **LPBF, ≥100 s⁻¹ uniaxial response, and a deliberately varied specimen test temperature**, start with **Ponnusamy et al.’s AlSi12 work**. For room-temperature high-rate constitutive data beyond AlSi10Mg, **Scalmalloy and Al6061** have particularly explicit reported measurements. Do not treat a printing-bed temperature, ageing schedule, or quasi-static elevated-temperature tensile curve as a high-rate temperature study. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000051)

(2021) directly measured LPBF Scalmalloy (AA5028, Al–Mg–Sc) tensile behavior at four strain rates from \(10^{-3}\) to \(1000\,s^{-1}\), including split-Hopkinson tension-bar tests. They tested both as-built and heat-treated specimens (325 °C for 4 h); yield stress was approximately 350 MPa as-built and 550 MPa after treatment. They analyzed ultimate tensile strength and failure strain using a simplified Johnson–Cook model. The excerpt describes heat treatment, not testing at different temperatures, and reports no other alloys.

contexts.context: Ponnusamy et al. (2018) studied **SLM AlSi12**, not AlSi10Mg or the alloys listed in the question. Fully dense ProX200 parts were tested in **compression** using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB), at **room temperature and 200°C**, alongside quasi-static compression at the same temperatures. The paper targets practical strain rates of approximately **10²–10⁴ s⁻¹** and reports a **negative strain-rate effect at room temperature** but a **positive strain-rate effect at 200°C**. It states that previously “no research seems to have been made” on dynamic behavior of SLM aluminum parts.

contexts.context: A 2018 study tested SLM-built **AlSi12** (an alloy other than AlSi10Mg) in compression using a split Hopkinson pressure bar. Ø8 × 8 mm specimens were tested quasi-statically at \(2\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) and dynamically at up to **750 s⁻¹** at room temperature, and up to **1500 s⁻¹** at **200°C** (specimen heated, bars kept at room temperature). Room-temperature tests showed a **negative strain-rate effect**, attributed to microcracks and adiabatic heating; at 200°C, a **positive strain-rate effect** was observed, associated with thermally activated diffusion and dynamic recrystallization.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports LPBF/SLM Scalmalloy tensile tests using servo-hydraulic and split-Hopkinson methods from \(10^{-3}\) to \(10^3\,s^{-1}\), covering the requested high-rate regime. As-built and heat-treated material were tested, but no test-temperature variation was performed: the model “only accounts for isotropic hardening but no temperature effects.” UTS decreased weakly (~5 MPa per decade), yield strength was rate-insensitive, and failure strain increased at \(10^3\,s^{-1}\), attributed likely to adiabatic heating. Parameters were given for both conditions, including \(a=-4.9\) and \(-2.9\) MPa.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides details for Ponnusamy et al. (2018), concerning selective-laser-melted (laser-powder-bed-fused) AlSi12 under compression. Cylindrical specimens were built horizontally on the SLM plate, then machined to 8 mm diameter × 8 mm height, giving an aspect ratio of 1.0. Quasi-static tests used a strain rate of 2 × 10^-3 s^-1; room-temperature SHPB tests reached 750 s^-1, while tests at 200 °C reached 1500 s^-1. The 200 °C condition was produced by heating only the specimen immediately before impact; the SHPB incident, transmission, and striker bars remained at room temperature. Thus, this is an initial specimen-temperature condition, not post-build heat treatment. At room temperature, the study reported a negative strain-rate effect, attributed to micro-cracks and adiabatic thermal softening. At 200 °C, it reported a positive strain-rate effect, associated with a rate-controlling thermally activated diffusion mechanism and possible dynamic recrystallization. The excerpt contains no information on a 2020 Ponnusamy study, 400 °C testing, post-build heat treatments, numerical simulations/effects, or comparative build orientations beyond stating that the specimens were built horizontally. It therefore cannot establish those requested details or distinguish additional thermal histories.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports PBF-LB **Al6061**, not AlSi10Mg. Quasi-static compression was conducted at \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Dynamic compression used a split Hopkinson pressure bar with 12.7-mm maraging-steel bars, high-speed imaging (0.5 million frames/s), and pulse shapers; at least three tests per condition covered nominal strain rates of \(5\times10^{2}\)–\(1.8\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Stress, strain, and strain rate were calculated using classical Kolsky equations. The excerpt describes no tensile SHPB tests and gives no test-temperature variation; specimens appear tested without reported temperature control.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports LPBF Al6061 compression testing, not AlSi10Mg or the specifically named alloys. Quasi-static rates (10⁻³–10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) were compared with dynamic rates of 500–800 and 1500–1800 s⁻¹ (approximately 1.75×10³ s⁻¹), apparently using Hopkinson-type testing. At 15% plastic strain, as-built flow stress increased from 296 MPa quasi-statically to 333 MPa dynamically; HIP increased from 193 to 231 MPa. Dynamic loading also reduced Poisson’s ratio (0.18–0.21 to 0.10–0.13). No test-temperature effects are reported.

It discusses tensile behavior at room and elevated temperatures after heat treatment. At 573 K, alloy C retained 45% of room-temperature strength, while alloy F retained 23%; strength loss was attributed to dislocation climb, grain-boundary sliding, and possible Mn-precipitate coarsening above 523 K. Alloy F contained 1.1 wt% Zr, with estimated precipitation-hardening contributions of 374 MPa versus 242 MPa for alloy C.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Has anyone measured the high-strain-rate (100 1/s or more, for example with a split Hopkinson bar) tensile or compressive response of laser powder bed fusion aluminum alloys other than AlSi10Mg, such as Scalmalloy, A20X/A205, AlSi7Mg, Al-Ce or Al-Fe-Zr alloys, including the effect of test temperature?

Yes. ## High-strain-rate measurements beyond AlSi10Mg

**Yes.** Published experiments establish high-rate tensile response for LPBF **Scalmalloy**, and compressive response for LPBF **AlSi12** and **Al6061**. A 2026 thesis additionally reports high-rate tension of two modified LPBF Al6061 materials. Of these verified studies, **AlSi12 is the clearest example in which specimen temperature was varied during high-rate testing**: split-Hopkinson compression was performed at room temperature and 200 °C. Ageing a specimen before a room-temperature test is a different experiment. (ponnusamy2018highstrainrate pages 1-3, ponnusamy2018highstrainrate pages 3-7, jakkula2021strainratesensitivity pages 1-2, yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 1-6, yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 17-21)

The verified experiments are summarized below. “Temperature” means the specimen’s temperature *during loading*, unless explicitly identified as a prior treatment. ### What the measurements show

- **Scalmalloy (AA5028):** Jakkula and colleagues used an EOS laser-powder-bed system and a split-Hopkinson **tension** bar. Their 2021 conference report and journal paper describe the same experimental programme, not two independent datasets: tests at approximately **1,000 s⁻¹**, with lower-rate comparators, on as-built and **325 °C/4 h pre-aged** material. At the high rate, the as-built and pre-aged ultimate tensile strengths were **342.5 ± 1.6** and **497.0 ± 3.0 MPa**, respectively; failure strains were **29.5 ± 0.4%** and **15.0 ± 2.2%**. All mechanical tests were at **room temperature**. Ultimate strength declined weakly as rate increased, whereas failure strain increased at the highest rate. The authors explicitly caution that their tests cannot disentangle intrinsic rate effects from adiabatic heating and call for experiments that vary *test* temperature at fixed rate. Their target 1,000 s⁻¹ rate was reached **after yield**, an important qualification when interpreting the reported yield stresses. (jakkula2021strainratesensitivity pages 1-2, jakkula2021strainratesensitivity pages 2-5, jakkula2021strainratesensitivity pages 5-7, jakkula2021strainratesensitivitya pages 1-3, jakkula2021strainratesensitivitya pages 3-6, jakkula2021strainratesensitivity media 0830a462)

- **AlSi12:** Ponnusamy and colleagues’ 2018 paper reports split-Hopkinson **compression** of horizontally built SLM cylinders, compared with quasi-static compression at the same specimen temperatures. Maximum dynamic rates were **750 s⁻¹ at room temperature** and **1,500 s⁻¹ at 200 °C**. For the hot test, they heated the **specimen**, leaving the bars at room temperature. They report a *negative* apparent rate effect at room temperature but a *positive* one at 200 °C; their stress–strain plots display those comparisons. Because the two dynamic temperature conditions also used **different maximum rates**, this is evidence of temperature-dependent high-rate response, **not** an isolated measurement of temperature dependence at one fixed high rate. A later paper entitled *Dynamic compressive behaviour of selective laser melted AlSi12 alloy: Effect of elevated temperature and heat treatment* (Ponnusamy et al., *Additive Manufacturing* **36**, 101614, 2020; DOI **10.1016/j.addma.2020.101614**) is another directly relevant lead, but its full text could not be verified here; no additional test temperatures or numerical outcomes are attributed to it. (ponnusamy2018highstrainrate pages 1-3, ponnusamy2018highstrainrate pages 3-7, ponnusamy2018highstrainrate media a89c0989, ponnusamy2018highstrainrate media c5e4830e)

- **Al6061:** Yilmaz and colleagues’ published study, *Mechanical behavior of Al6061 produced by laser powder bed fusion: Effects of heat treatments and strain rates* (*Materials Science and Engineering A* **950**, 149574, 2026; DOI **10.1016/j.msea.2025.149574**), is reproduced as a chapter of Yilmaz’s accessible 2026 thesis. It reports split-Hopkinson **compression at 500–800 and 1,500–1,800 s⁻¹**. At 15% plastic strain and the higher rate, flow stress was **333 ± 6 MPa as-built**, **348 ± 17 MPa direct-aged**, **246 ± 6 MPa annealed**, **238 ± 9 MPa T6**, and **231 ± 5 MPa after HIP**. Each condition had a higher flow stress under dynamic than quasi-static loading. These are comparisons of **prior thermal treatments at room-temperature test conditions**, not high-rate tests performed at the heat-treatment temperatures. The material retained approximately **3.5–5% porosity**, limiting generalization to denser LPBF Al6061. (yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 1-6, yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 39-43, yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior media 2ccf574d, yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 17-21, yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 21-25)

- **Modified Al6061:** A separate chapter of that thesis, described there as **submitted for publication**, reports room-temperature split-Hopkinson **tension** on LPBF Al6061 mixed with **0.3 wt% Sc** and on ceramic-inoculated **Al6061–RAM2**. The Sc material reached about **600 s⁻¹**, with **33 ± 8 MPa** ultimate strength and **0.5 ± 0.1%** elongation; severe interconnected porosity caused premature fracture. RAM2 reached **2,700 s⁻¹**, with **239 ± 3 MPa** ultimate strength and **21.0 ± 2.0%** elongation. These formulations are **not Scalmalloy or A205/A20X**, and the thesis does not vary their specimen test temperature. (yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 49-53, yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 53-57, yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 57-61, yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 61-64, yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior media 1dc0cfa3)

### Status of the other named alloys

I did **not identify a verified ≥100 s⁻¹ tensile or compressive test on LPBF A20X/A205, AlSi7Mg (A356/A357), an Al–Ce alloy, or Al–Fe–Zr**. This is a statement about the located literature, **not proof that no unpublished or unindexed measurement exists**. The distinction matters because several close-looking results fail the rate criterion: the LPBF **Al–Fe–Zr** report gives room-temperature tensile properties after **400 °C/4 h ageing**, not high-rate tests; LPBF **Al–Ce** literature reports elevated-temperature tensile strength and thermal exposure, but not a verified qualifying Hopkinson test; and the surveyed A356/A357 literature emphasizes tensile, fatigue and shear properties rather than qualifying high-rate uniaxial measurements. A 2025 LPBF **Al–Fe–Cr–X** study actually varied *test* temperature from room temperature to 400 °C, but its compression strain-rate steps were only **10⁻⁵–10⁻² s⁻¹**. Likewise, LPBF Al–Mn–Cr–Zr was tensile-tested up to 573 K, including a rate comparison reaching **1% s⁻¹ = 0.01 s⁻¹**—far below 100 s⁻¹. (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4, liu2024reviewoflaser pages 23-25, pauzon2022anovellaser pages 4-8, baharisambran2025dynamicandstatic pages 4-6, ponnusamy2020mechanicalpropertiesof pages 40-42, ponnusamy2020mechanicalpropertiesof pages 38-40, mehta2024mechanicalpropertiesand pages 4-5)

**Bottom line:** For the specific combination of **LPBF, ≥100 s⁻¹ uniaxial response, and a deliberately varied specimen test temperature**, start with **Ponnusamy et al.’s AlSi12 work**. For room-temperature high-rate constitutive data beyond AlSi10Mg, **Scalmalloy and Al6061** have particularly explicit reported measurements. Do not treat a printing-bed temperature, ageing schedule, or quasi-static elevated-temperature tensile curve as a high-rate temperature study. (ponnusamy2018highstrainrate pages 3-7, jakkula2021strainratesensitivity pages 2-5, yilmaz2026strainratedependentmechanicalbehavior pages 39-43, pauzon2022anovellaser pages 4-8, mehta2024mechanicalpropertiesand pages 4-5)
